title: Avoid Red Ocean Traps
coreMove: Spot when a strategic move has become competitor-first or existing-demand-first, then pull the question back to buyer value and new demand.
sourcePressure: Close by warning against relapse into red-ocean logic: benchmarking rivals, fighting over existing demand, technology-first moves, niche-only thinking, and imitation disguised as strategy.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Treating red-ocean traps as a list of bad tactics rather than a mindset that turns useful tools into imitation.

sourceAnchors.name: red ocean strategy
sourceAnchors.detail: official support defines red ocean strategy as competition for existing demand in known market space
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Red ocean strategy begins when the known market and existing demand quietly become the edge of imagination.

sourceAnchors.name: strategist mindset support
sourceAnchors.detail: official support warns that benchmarking rivals and fighting over existing customers pull leaders back toward red-ocean logic
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Benchmarking is useful as information and dangerous as imagination; the trap is letting rivals choose the question.

hook: Do not open with a competitor scoreboard, a war metaphor, or a generic market map.
Do not use A crowded market is not..., The real strategy is..., or What if growth... as reusable shells.
counterintuition: Avoid Most people assume... but actually... and The opposite is true.
Avoid turning every chapter into competition bad, creativity good.
tryThisNow: Avoid Set a timer for 60 seconds and list... as a repeated action.
Avoid generic reflect on your strategy prompts.
examples: Avoid conference-room whiteboard workshops as the default scene.
Avoid repeating mugs, markers, dosing cups, bike helmets, radiators, bus depots, classrooms, narrow kitchens, or generic dashboard scenes.

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person You direct address, retrospective It took her three weeks to see, question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm: a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'

exampleSpecs.domain: competitor dashboard framing versus buyer-value search
exampleSpecs.audience: a leader whose team benchmarks itself into imitation
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the review starts with buyer value or rival reaction
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he keeps competitor data in the room but refuses to let it set the opening frame
exampleSpecs.firstImage: The competitor dashboard refreshes in blue light across David's face

exampleSpecs.domain: ticket kiosk biometric payment versus refund recovery
exampleSpecs.audience: a product lead tempted by face-scan payment
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether innovation solves the real user pain or decorates it
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she sees that biometric payment does not solve the refund problem buyers care about
exampleSpecs.firstImage: At 10:18 a.m., Margaux watches a traveler tap the refund button six times
mustAvoid: generic airport kiosk scene from chapter 4

exampleSpecs.domain: specialty travel niche narrowing and stalled demand
exampleSpecs.audience: a founder serving expert birders while missing broader family demand
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the company grows or fights over a tiny expert pool
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he reconstructs how finer segmentation shrank demand instead of opening it
exampleSpecs.firstImage: It took Niklas four perfect birding itineraries to see the same twelve names booking again

exampleSpecs.domain: campus marketplace speed without utility change
exampleSpecs.audience: a student entrepreneur racing a rival team
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether speed creates value or only an early launch
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: his early launch wins attention but students return to old behavior because utility gaps remain
exampleSpecs.firstImage: "We launched first," Chidi says, then watches three students exchange textbooks in the hallway anyway

exampleSpecs.domain: premium luggage details that raise cost without utility
exampleSpecs.audience: a product designer pressured to make a suitcase stand out
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether added features raise buyer value or only cost
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the costly detail looks different but does not help the buyer's airport job
exampleSpecs.firstImage: The sample room smells like new nylon and cut foam around Tomas's open suitcase shell

exampleSpecs.domain: clinic wound-care tray cost cuts that harm utility
exampleSpecs.audience: an operator trying to lower supply cost without harming care
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether low cost supports value or hollows it out
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she predicts the cheaper tray works, then a nurse loses time rebuilding missing pieces
exampleSpecs.firstImage: What if the cheaper tray saves four dollars and costs seven minutes at the bedside?

skillTargets: evaluate technology, niche, speed, and cost moves by buyer value and new demand

tryThisNowSpec: Look at one current initiative and ask whether the first sentence names a rival, a technology, or a buyer pain.
